This keys off idea 4e670c74 (QA in the pull request loop), where the missing piece turned out to be knowing who the other humans are rather than moving code between machines. The peer-to-peer layer is still wanted and still the real answer; this is what a team could run on before it exists.\\n\\nThe idea is that Jira, or GitHub issues, becomes the coordination surface. Assignment in the tracker is how work is claimed. For a Jira-backed project, hall9k finds the Jira items assigned to this user and adopts a hall9k task for each one, so a person\\u0027s board fills itself from the tracker rather than from a local act.\\n\\nThe existing paths stay. A user can still create Jira cards from hall9k, and can still adopt a Jira item that is not assigned to them. What is new is a project setting along the lines of: do not claim a hall9k task until its Jira item is assigned to this user. And the reverse direction, so claiming is not a two-place act: when the user decides to claim a hall9k task, hall9k tells Jira to assign that item to them. The tracker and the board stay in agreement because one command moves both.\\n\\nThe same shape applies to GitHub issues, though that is a different beast and less urgent, because the next big team project is in Jira.\\n\\nWhy this matters beyond convenience: each person runs their own hall9k install against their own database, and the tracker is the only shared state. That gives a team assignment and identity with no shared infrastructure and no peer-to-peer layer. It is also what makes 4e670c74 reachable early, since the branch is already on the shared git remote by the time a pull request exists, so another person\\u0027s machine can fetch it and cut a worktree with machinery that already works. A sweep that continuously discovers newly assigned items makes that rule feel different: discovery becomes continuous while content stays frozen. Worth confirming that a team would agree assignment is not workflow.\\n- GitHub issue assignees have to be repository collaborators, which Jira does not require. A human doing a strict code review creates a pr-review task, which is the answer the platform already has. That task can be linked to the original task so the two are aware of each other, which is fine and is not the hard part.\\n\\nThe real kicker is QA. At ARX-5555 there is a QA team with no defined place in this loop, and the pull request is the spot. Today the pull request is strictly a code review: it gets reviewed, approved, and merged into main, and only then does the work become a Jira task for QA. QA picks it up, and the build has to be completed and deployed into staging and test before they can touch it. So main accumulates merged work that nobody has actually exercised.\\n\\nInstead, or in addition, two things happen during the pull request review phase, in parallel. One is the ordinary code review by another developer; in the concrete case, I assign my pull request to Sarah and she reviews the code. The other is a QA person reviewing the same pull request, but not as a code review. They review it as actual QA. They assign the task to themselves and claim it, which takes the claim away from me, and they pull. Hall9k sets up the worktree on their machine, gets it ready, and their machine runs it. They QA it in their own environment before anything merges to main.\\n\\nThe consequences are what make it worth building. Anything in main is releasable at any point, because nothing merges that QA has not already exercised. We can still keep a staging and test environment, but it stops being the gate. QA runs everything from their local environment and does not have to be a developer to do it, because hall9k does the setup that would otherwise require one. And if the QA person wants to write automated tests that belong to the repo, they add those tests to the branch: either as part of the same pull request, or as a stacked pull request sitting on top of the original one.\\n\\nThat also sidesteps a pile of infrastructure work. We do not have to figure out how Azure DevOps spins up a CI container and everything around it just to give QA something to test against. Maybe we still want that eventually, but in the meantime hall9k can do the setup for the QA person and we go from there.\\n\\nOpen questions for discovery, not decided here:\\n\\n- A claim today is per-machine and per-human, and a task reaches Done when the pull request opens. QA taking the claim after Done needs a story for what state the task is in while QA holds it, and whether QA is claiming the original task at all or a QA task of its own that is linked to it, the way a pr-review task is.\\n- Moving a branch and its worktree to another person\\u0027s machine is the peer-to-peer layer, which is designed and unbuilt. This idea probably cannot be built before that is, unless it takes a shared-remote path that does not depend on it.\\n- Stacked pull requests are not something the platform has any notion of yet.\\n- Whether a QA verdict blocks the merge, and if so where that verdict is recorded, given that the platform never merges.\\n- When QA does its local walkthrough, the branch probably needs to be rebased onto the current origin/main first, so QA is exercising the change on top of releasable state rather than on top of whatever main looked like when the branch was cut. Worth tackling in discovery, including what it costs: a rebase rewrites the branch a pull request is already open on, which forces a push and moves the diff a code reviewer may already be partway through. It also only narrows the window rather than closing it, since main can move again between the QA pass and the merge, so the guarantee is that the change was QA\\u0027d against main as of that moment, not against the eventual merge commit. Closing it completely is a merge queue, which is a much larger Today a task\\u0027s whole life belongs to one node: my node (or I, interactively) claim it, do the work, and the daemon opens the pull request. Everything after that is outside hall9k\\u0027s model except closeout monitoring. In a team project, where multiple people work the same repository (whatever the distributed shared-project system turns out to be), two pieces are missing.\\n\\nFirst, handoff. The work runs to the pull request on one node, and then it has to be handed to other humans. When the pull request opens, humans get assigned to it in GitHub, one or several, and each of them can take it on their own.\\n\\nSecond, what a reviewer\\u0027s participation is in hall9k\\u0027s own terms. A human doing a strict code review creates a pr-review task, which is the answer the platform already has. That task can be linked to the original task so the two are aware of each other, which is fine and is not the hard part.\\n\\nThe real kicker is QA. At ARX-5555 there is a QA team with no defined place in this loop, and the pull request is the spot. Today the pull request is strictly a code review: it gets reviewed, approved, and merged into main, and only then does the work become a Jira task for QA. QA picks it up, and the build has to be completed and deployed into staging and test before they can touch it. So main accumulates merged work that nobody has actually exercised.\\n\\nInstead, or in addition, two things happen during the pull request review phase, in parallel. One is the ordinary code review by another developer; in the concrete case, I assign my pull request to Sarah and she reviews the code. The other is a QA person reviewing the same pull request, but not as a code review. They review it as actual QA. They assign the task to themselves and claim it, which takes the claim away from me, and they pull. Hall9k sets up the worktree on their machine, gets it ready, and their machine runs it. They QA it in their own environment before anything merges to main.\\n\\nThe consequences are what make it worth building. Anything in main is releasable at any point, because nothing merges that QA has not already exercised. We can still keep a staging and test environment, but it stops being the gate. QA runs everything from their local environment and does not have to be a developer to do it, because hall9k does the setup that would otherwise require one. And if the QA person wants to write automated tests that belong to the repo, they add those tests to the branch: either as part of the same pull request, or as a stacked pull request sitting on top of the original one.\\n\\nThat also sidesteps a pile of infrastructure work. We do not have to figure out how Azure DevOps spins up a CI container and everything around it just to give QA something to test against. Maybe we still want that eventually, but in the meantime hall9k can do the setup for the QA person and we go from there.\\n\\nOpen questions for discovery, not decided here:\\n\\n- A claim today is per-machine and per-human, and a task reaches Done when the pull request opens. QA taking the claim after Done needs a story for what state the task is in while QA holds it, and whether QA is claiming the original task at all or a QA task of its own that is linked to it, the way a pr-review task is.\\n- Moving a branch and its worktree to another person\\u0027s machine is the peer-to-peer layer, which is designed and unbuilt. This idea probably cannot be built before that is, unless it takes a shared-remote path that does not depend on it.\\n- Stacked pull requests are not something the platform has any notion of yet.\\n- Whether a QA verdict blocks the merge, and if so where that verdict is recorded, given that the platform never merges.\\n- When QA does its local walkthrough, the branch probably needs to be rebased onto the current origin/main first, so QA is exercising the change on top of releasable state rather than on top of whatever main looked like when the branch was cut. Worth tackling in discovery, including what it costs: a rebase rewrites the branch a pull request is already open on, which forces a push and moves the diff a code reviewer may already be partway through. It also only narrows the window rather than closing it, since main can move again between the QA pass and the merge, so the guarantee is that the change was QA\\u0027d against main as of that moment, not against the eventual merge commit. Closing it completely is a merge queue, which is a much larger thing.\\n- Sequencing, and the hole in it. The shape being considered is that a reviewer\\u0027s approval is what makes the pull request eligible for QA, rather than eligible for merge. Sarah approves, the branch is rebased onto the current origin/main as the first step of QA\\u0027s own process, and QA then takes it on sitting on top of main, so what they approve is not so stale that merging it introduces problems that were never exercised. The hole is that in GitHub an approved pull request is immediately mergeable, by anyone with the button, and hall9k has no way to say \\u0022approved but not yet releasable\\u0022. Something has to hold the merge shut between approval and QA sign-off. Worth checking in discovery whether that is a required status check that hall9k publishes and leaves pending until QA signs off, or simply branch protection requiring a second approval from a QA reviewer, which needs no custom machinery at all. Not a blocker, but it needs an answer before the sequence means anything.\\n- The review pass after the rebase. Rebasing invalidates the FinalFullPass that ran immediately before the pull request opened, and the platform\\u0027s existing rule is that nothing reaches the remote on delta-green alone, so a post-rebase pass is restoring an invariant rather than adding a nicety. The likely split is that the gates (build, test) run at full scope, because the tree genuinely changed, while the review itself is deliberately lighter than a Discovery cycle: closer in shape to the Verify cycle (Decisions Log #92, #105), asking whether the rebase broke anything rather than rediscovering the diff, with a high bar for a finding to earn a fix What exists already and is NOT this idea: per-role models for review, fix, and verify (#33, #82, #105) settable at node/project/task; cycle caps and the lifetime budget (e5c0d371, landing). What is genuinely new: (1) stage toggles - build with no review at all, adversarial-only, conformance-only, skip the final full pass - composed per project or task; (2) the one missing model knob, a separately configurable final-full-pass model; (3) the Adjudicate stage: a short-lived fresh-context pass on the strongest model, slotted between a review verdict and the fix dispatch, ruling each finding in, out, or park-for-human on the merits, reading the findings and their cited lines only, NEVER the branch diff (the #94 packet lesson; the 576M-token day is what diff-scoped passes cost). Field support for Adjudicate: findings-triage filter agents are among the better-replicated results in multi-agent review (an SAST filter agent measured 88.6 percent false-positive reduction at 3.1 percent recall cost; a commercial micro-agent system reports 51 percent). Two design requirements from our own scars: every run records the stage configuration it ran under (the stranding investigation took three rounds because nothing on the stream said which prompt a session ran - experiments are unreadable without provenance), and defaults stay the full pipeline with load-bearing guarantees (#92, #98) removable only with the consequence said out loud at set time - the platform advises, never refuses, same doctrine as idea fcaded0b. Measurement gates before building Adjudicate: (a) the store already holds ground-truth labels for the false-finding rate - every human park ruling is one (dismissed merge-ready means a wasted lap was coming; upheld needs-fixes means the reviewer was right) - so measure that rate first and only build if it clears the breakeven (a scoped arbiter pass costs a small fraction of the fix-session-plus-verify-lap-plus-gate a bogus Medium costs); (b) judge against the post-d74c353d baseline, since the final-pass fix bar removes the largest measured slice of wasted laps already; (c) Adjudicate ships with a pre-committed revert condition, because 93 percent of finding locations appear in exactly one run, so a wrongly discarded finding is likely never rediscovered. Explicitly rejected during exploration: keeping reviewer agents resident for live dialogue with the fix agent - the field\\u0027s own design requirement is context asymmetry (a critic inheriting the builder\\u0027s context defeats independence), hall9k\\u0027s fresh-context-per-cycle doctrine says the same, and the findings and fix-position artifacts already carry the dialogue (dispute parks are the fix session challenging the reviewer today).
